RESEARCH ONLY — do not write or modify any code, do not create report .md files. Return findings as your final assistant message text.

Context: We're building "NxLabs" — a mod / plugin / shader / texture-pack / world-save catalog AND one-click server-side installer inside a game-server + VPS hosting business (Nxeon, ~47 game families). I need a sharp, opinionated competitive UX teardown to steal the good ideas and beat the bad ones.

Part A — Mod CATALOG sites. Study the actual live UX of:
- Modrinth (modrinth.com) — search/facets, project pages, version selector, dependency display, creator monetization program (they pay authors — find the details and the payout model), their "Modrinth App" launcher.
- CurseForge (curseforge.com) — search, the Overwolf app, the author rewards program (find how it works, the pool, the per-download rate), ads/paywalls, the "allowModDistribution" third-party download restriction and how it shows up for users.
- Thunderstore (thunderstore.io) — package pages, communities, dependency strings, the Thunderstore Mod Manager.
- Nexus Mods (nexusmods.com) — premium/free download gating, collections feature (this is a big one — Nexus "Collections" = curated mod lists with load order and config; understand it well), Donation Points system, the Vortex manager.
For each: what specifically is good about the browse→understand→install flow, and what's genuinely bad/annoying.

Part B — GAME HOSTING PANELS' one-click mod install. This is the more important half. Study how these actually do it and what the user sees:
- Pterodactyl / Pelican panel egg ecosystem (how eggs handle modpack installs, the "install script" model, Pterodactyl mod install add-ons/plugins)
- Apex Hosting (their "one-click modpack installer" / Apex panel — they market this heavily)
- Shockbyte, BisectHosting (their "one-click modpack install" and JAR switcher), GGServers, PebbleHost, Nodecraft, Nitrado, GPortal, Hostinger game hosting
- AMP (CubeCoders) and its mod handling
- Any panel with a built-in Modrinth/CurseForge browser (e.g. Pterodactyl mod manager plugins, Crafty Controller, MCSManager)

For each, report specifically how they handle:
(a) version/compatibility matching between a mod and the server's game version + mod loader (Forge/Fabric/NeoForge/Quilt/Paper/Spigot) — do they filter, warn, or just let it break?
(b) dependency resolution — automatic? manual? none?
(c) conflicting mods / duplicate detection
(d) showing required RAM / resource impact of a modpack
(e) reviews/ratings/social proof
(f) creator/author programs and revenue share
(g) what happens on a server that's already running — restart handling, backup-before-install, rollback
(h) world/save compatibility warnings (installing a mod into an existing world)

Part C — Opinionated synthesis. What do ALL of them do badly that a new entrant could beat them on? Be specific and concrete, not generic. Think about things like: no cross-game unified catalog, no "will this actually run on your 4GB plan" answer, no rollback, no dependency hell resolution, no mod conflict detection, no automated compatibility testing, license opacity, broken search, no mod profiles/presets, no "restore my server to before this mod" button, no per-mod performance telemetry. Rank the opportunities by how much they'd actually matter to a customer.

Use WebSearch and WebFetch extensively. Look at real docs, real marketing pages, real forum/Reddit complaints about these products (Reddit threads about "Apex one click modpack broken", "Pterodactyl mod install", "BisectHosting modpack", etc. are gold for finding what's bad). Cite URLs for factual claims about features and programs. Distinguish clearly between what you verified and what is your own judgment.

## Adding Mods to Existing Worlds

Most mods like inventory editors and mini-maps shouldn't have any effect on the world save, but it's always a good idea to have a backup in case the mod crashes the game, which has a slight chance of corrupting the world.

## Removing Mods and Missing Blocks

When you remove a mod that added content to your world, if a mod added custom block types that were used in the world and then the mod is uninstalled, the custom blocks get deleted from the world and inventory/chests when the world is opened without the mod.

World corruption from mod removal is not recoverable by any other means, and the failure often does not appear immediately — a world can load fine and then break when you walk into an area that used the removed mod.

When it gets to a notification, type /fml confirm to tell Forge that you really do intend to delete the old content from the mods that you removed. This is the proper way to handle missing blocks when using Forge mod loader.
